briefing.text: Who counts as 'SV-driven TXR1 target-mediated activation' has to be decided from the data, not read off one column. High TXR1 expression alone, or the mere presence of a reported junction, mixes in non-driving SVs and lineage-driven high expression: most SVs near a gene do not change its expression, and only promoter-facing enhancer-hijack rearrangements activate it. Check: cross-tabulate breakpoint_topology (P2T versus INV/D2T/NONE) against txr1_log_tpm, lineage_marker_log_tpm, target_ase_alt_fraction and phase_consistency, and see whether high-TXR1 cases without P2T are explained by lineage expression or copy number. If so, define the target population from mechanism-consistent evidence across modalities (P2T topology plus adequate alt_molecule_fraction plus haplotype-consistent ASE/phase), and report how the estimates move under alternative definitions.
briefing.reason: The target population definition decides which patients enter every estimate; a wrong definition changes all four reported numbers.

briefing.text: Some reported P2T junctions may be artifacts. Long-read SV calls at loci with segmental duplication, high homology or low complexity are often false positives from mis-mapping to paralogous copies. Check: among P2T calls, by platform, look at mapq_median, segmental_dup_overlap, homology_bp, low_complexity_score, split_molecule_count, molecule_depth and read_n50; flag P2T calls with low MAPQ or high segmental-duplication overlap that also lack expression, ASE or phase support. If found: treat artifact-prone calls as not SV-driven, or as uncertain with sensitivity analyses that include and exclude them, instead of trusting the topology label.
briefing.reason: False-positive SV calls would put non-target tumors into the target population and dilute the effect estimate.

briefing.text: Raw allele fractions (alt_molecule_fraction, target_ase_alt_fraction) are diluted by low tumor purity and distorted by local copy-number gain or whole-genome doubling. A true clonal SV in a low-purity sample can look weak, and amplification can raise TXR1 expression or mimic allelic imbalance with no SV. Check: plot alt_molecule_fraction and the ASE fraction against tumor_purity, local_total_copy, tumor_ploidy and wgd_flag; check whether high TXR1 expression in non-P2T cases tracks local_total_copy. If found: adjust the fractions for purity and copy number (expected fraction is roughly purity x mutant copies / total copies) before applying any threshold, so low-purity true SVs are not excluded; do not count amplification-only activation as SV-driven.
briefing.reason: A fixed raw-fraction threshold would wrongly exclude low-purity true SV cases and could admit amplification-only cases, shifting target membership.

briefing.text: Expression features (txr1_log_tpm, ASE) can be shifted by expression_batch, rna_quality and library size, and baseline TXR1 expression correlates with the lineage program, so fixed expression cut-offs misclassify cases. Misclassified subgroup membership biases the subgroup effect toward the effect in the misclassified group, usually toward the null. Check: compare txr1_log_tpm and housekeeping_log_tpm across expression_batch and rna_quality; regress TXR1 on lineage_marker_log_tpm to get lineage-adjusted residual expression; check how stable subgroup membership is under alternative definitions. If found: normalize within batch, use lineage-adjusted expression only as supporting evidence, and report effect estimates under a stricter and a looser subgroup definition.
briefing.reason: Batch and lineage effects on expression could misclassify who is in the target population if expression is used as evidence.

briefing.text: Keep eligibility, treatment assignment and time zero aligned. Use only analysis_set==1 as the time-zero cohort, check time_zero_day, and confirm every covariate used for adjustment is measured at baseline. Post-baseline variables such as assessed16 and tox_stop_8wk must never go into the treatment (confounder) model or be used to restrict the cohort: that causes selection, immortal-time and collider bias. Post-baseline events are handled through the missingness model, not through eligibility.
briefing.reason: Choosing the wrong cohort or adjusting for post-treatment variables biases the benefit estimate.

briefing.text: Treatment choice in the registry is not random: it is likely confounded by ECOG, tumor burden, prior lines/resistance, lineage, site and calendar period. Within the target population nearly everyone may have received TXR1i, so inverse-probability weights can become extreme or the comparison may lack data support. Check, within the target population: propensity-score overlap by arm, maximum/minimum weights, effective sample size, weighted standardized mean differences (aim below 0.1) for all baseline confounders, and structural non-positivity (for example a site or period with no non-TXR1 systemic-therapy patients). If found: use a doubly robust estimator, report the region with overlap, and say explicitly if trimming or overlap weights move the estimand away from the full target population; never trim silently.
briefing.reason: A crude arm comparison is confounded, and poor overlap can make a weighted estimate unstable or change the population it refers to.

briefing.text: The benefit estimand 'as if all patients had an assessable week-16 visit' is a hypothetical estimand. A complete-case analysis that drops assessed16==0 is biased if non-assessment depends on prognosis or on treatment toxicity; early toxicity discontinuation is a likely cause of missing week-16 visits under TXR1i. Check: tabulate assessed16 by therapy_class, tox_stop_8wk, ecog, tumor_burden, site and calendar_period, and fit a model for P(assessed16=1 | treatment, baseline covariates). If non-assessment is non-random: use inverse-probability-of-missingness weights multiplied by the treatment weights, or g-computation/AIPW, under missing-at-random given covariates; state that this assumption cannot be tested and run a delta/tipping-point sensitivity analysis. Do not impute non-assessed patients as failures: that answers a composite estimand, not the one asked for.
briefing.reason: How missing week-16 outcomes are handled determines whether the estimate matches the estimand the task names.

briefing.text: The requested benefit number is a standardized marginal risk difference in percentage points within the target population. TXR1i benefit is likely concentrated in true SV-driven tumors (effect modification), so an estimate over the whole registry, or a conditional measure such as a logistic-regression odds ratio or coefficient, is not what is asked. Check by estimating the effect separately in target and non-target groups. Fit the models within the target population, or with treatment-by-target interactions, and marginalize over the target population's covariate distribution. Bootstrap the whole pipeline (missingness weights, propensity, outcome and toxicity models) for confidence intervals and carry the uncertainty into net utility = benefit RD - 0.35 x toxicity risk.
briefing.reason: Reporting a pooled or conditional effect instead of the target-population marginal risk difference gives the wrong quantity.

briefing.text: The 8-week toxicity/discontinuation risk asked for is a marginal risk under TXR1i over the whole target population, including those who actually received other therapy. A crude tox_stop_8wk rate among TXR1i-treated patients is biased if their germline DLR1 status or clinical makeup differs from the whole target population. Toxicity under TXR1i probably depends on DLR1 metabolizer status: compute an activity score as the sum of the two haplotype activity values from dlr1_allele_table instead of treating each star allele as its own category; tabulate tox_stop_8wk by activity score under TXR1i; check dlr1_call_confidence and ancestry_group. Estimate the risk by standardizing (g-computation or IPW) over the whole target population's covariates, activity score included, and handle low-confidence diplotype calls with a sensitivity analysis or multiple imputation.
briefing.reason: The toxicity term enters net utility directly; a crude treated-only rate or mishandled pharmacogene coding would misstate it.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that, among P2T calls that pass the artifact filter, a sizeable group has high TXR1 copy number and/or a low junction alt allele fraction, and treated these as a separate group when deciding who has SV-driven target-mediated activation. Your notes say you checked purity/copy-adjusted alt fraction, but your stated target definition uses only artifact flags, ASE and phase. Check in your data how copy number and purity-adjusted junction allele fraction are distributed among your target cases, and whether cases with amplification or a subclonal junction behave like the rest of your target. Does that change who belongs in your target population?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: you reported that your doubly robust estimate was unstable (low control effective sample size, a very large maximum combined weight) and that your result depends on the estimator. The other team did not record that instability in its target population. Check where your extreme weights come from: which patients carry them, whether they come from the treatment model or the assessment model, and whether they concentrate in a subgroup of your target that could be defined by tumour-genomic features. Does what you find change your target definition or your choice of primary estimator?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that a small number of target cases have a low-confidence DLR1 call and checked whether excluding them moved the toxicity risk and the benefit estimate. Your records show no check of DLR1 call confidence. Check whether low-confidence calls exist in your target and whether the activity score is reliable for them. Does it change how you standardize the toxicity risk?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team flagged artifact-prone P2T calls using segmental-duplication overlap together with breakpoint homology length and low-complexity fraction, and arrived at a somewhat different count of excluded calls than your segdup-plus-MAPQ rule. Check which P2T calls the two kinds of rule would classify differently in your data and whether those calls look like true junctions. Does it change your artifact filter?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that its doubly robust estimate of the benefit difference was unstable: the product of treatment and assessment weights gave a low effective sample size in the comparator arm and a very large maximum weight, and the point estimate differed noticeably from its bootstrap median and from outcome-model standardization. You clipped assessment probabilities at a floor. Check in your target the effective sample size per arm, the maximum combined weight, how many patients hit the clip, and how far your estimate moves with no clipping, with other clip levels, and with pure outcome-model standardization. Does it change which estimator you treat as primary?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team defined the target population without a copy-number or junction-clonality requirement, using artifact flags plus ASE and phase support, and chose its cut-offs from the bimodal distributions of the molecular features alone. You wrote that your thresholds were informed partly by naive outcome patterns within strata. Check whether your copy-number and alt-fraction cut-offs can be justified from the molecular data alone (for example after adjusting allele fraction for purity and local copy number), without looking at benefit by stratum, and whether amplified or low-allele-fraction cases that still show haplotype-linked expression are really not SV-driven target-mediated activation. Does it change who belongs in your target population?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team checked treatment positivity within site-by-period cells and weighted standardized mean differences after adjustment, and recorded that confounded treatment assignment and purity/copy distortion of allele fractions were both present in the data and changed its method. Your records show a propensity range and batch balance only. Check positivity by site and calendar period and covariate balance after weighting inside your target, and whether your raw alt-fraction cut-off is distorted by tumour purity or copy number. Does it change your confounder set or your target criteria?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team standardized the TXR1i toxicity risk over the whole target population (both arms) with the DLR1 activity score entered as a categorical variable, because the toxicity rate changed sharply and non-linearly across score levels. Check how you coded the activity score, whether a linear term fits the observed toxicity by score level in your data, and over which patients you averaged the predicted TXR1i toxicity. Does it change your toxicity estimate's method?

referee.difference: Both teams use the same estimands and similar estimators (AIPW/g-computation, MAR given covariates, arm and 8-week toxicity; toxicity standardized over the target under TXR1i), and their toxicity risks are close (33.5 vs 34.9). The difference is the rows kept, i.e. how 'SV-driven TXR1 target-mediated activation' is read. X's target (n=481) is a strict subset of Y's (n=666). X also requires a clonal junction (purity/copy-corrected CCF>=0.55), no high-level gain (local copy<=3.6) and stricter ASE/phase cut-offs. Y keeps the 185 extra P2T cases, which are mostly high-copy (median 5.3) with a subclonal junction (median CCF 0.30). Including them lowers the benefit RD from about 29 to about 17pp.
referee.test: work/test1.py: fit TXR1 expression on copy, lineage marker, purity and batch in NONE-topology cases, then compare residual expression in the core (X and Y) group and the disputed (Y-only) group. work/test2.py: within each group, separately estimate the adjusted week-16 benefit RD (g-computation integrating over an arm-specific 8-week toxicity model, all-assessed hypothetical estimand) with a 150-rep bootstrap, plus the standardized TXR1i toxicity.
referee.expected_if_x: If X is right (the disputed cases are copy-gain or subclonal and not driven through the target), the disputed group should show a TXR1i benefit effect near zero and clearly below the core's, and weaker SV-linked expression.
referee.expected_if_y: If Y is right (the disputed cases are true SV-driven activation hidden by purity/copy dilution), the disputed group should show a benefit RD similar to the core's (about 25-30pp) and comparable SV-linked expression.
referee.outcome: Benefit RD was +24.7pp (bootstrap 95% CI 13.0 to 35.2) in the core (n=481) and -10.4pp (CI -18.0 to +6.9) in the disputed group (n=185); complete-case crude RD was +28.6 vs -5.6. Toxicity under TXR1i was similar (33.2 vs 28.8). Excess TXR1 expression over NONE cases was +1.99 log units in the core and +1.15 in the disputed group, and within the disputed group it correlated with CCF (r=0.53; r=0.02 in the core). This fits partial, subclonal activation rather than the clonal target-mediated state.
referee.reason: The disputed cases show no TXR1i benefit, and the CI excludes the core effect. Their junction is subclonal or amplified and their expression excess is only partial. So Y's broader target mixes in a non-responsive, non-target-mediated subgroup that dilutes the estimand. Both teams agree on the toxicity component and on code 1, so the dispute is the benefit size: X's 29.1pp and net 17.4pp are supported. Caveat: the test uses outcomes to arbitrate a target definition. X's cut-offs were set on molecular grounds (a bimodal CCF gap), and the expression test, which is outcome-free, points the same way.
